Getting into houseplants is easier than it looks—you just want to start simple and avoid the “I’ll buy ten at once” trap.

First, figure out your light. This matters more than anything else. Spend a day noticing which windows get strong sun (south/west), gentle light (east), or barely any direct light (north). The plant you choose has to match this, not the other way around.

Then pick a few beginner-friendly plants that match your space:
- Low light: snake plant, ZZ plant, pothos  
- Medium/bright indirect light: pothos, philodendron, spider plant, peace lily  
- Bright light: succulents, cacti, fiddle leaf fig (a bit fussier)

Start with 2–3 plants max so you can actually pay attention to them.

Watering is where most people go wrong. The rule isn’t “once a week,” it’s “when the soil needs it.” Stick your finger into the soil about an inch:
- Dry? Water thoroughly until it drains out the bottom  
- Still damp? Leave it alone  

Overwatering kills way more plants than underwatering.

Make sure your pots have drainage holes. If water can’t escape, roots rot. If you like decorative pots, keep the plant in a plastic nursery pot inside it and take it out to water.

Use basic indoor potting mix—nothing fancy needed at the start. Fertilizer is optional early on; you can add a general liquid fertilizer every month or so in spring/summer once you’re comfortable.

A couple extra tips that save headaches:
- Don’t move plants around constantly; they like consistency  
- Wipe dust off leaves occasionally so they can “breathe”  
- Check for pests (tiny bugs, sticky residue) every week or so  
- Expect a little trial and error—losing a plant or two is normal
